name: Z-function prefix match length scan
definition: For n=0 return []; otherwise z_0=0 and [l,r)=[0,0); for i=1,…,n−1 set z_i=min(r−i,z_{i−l}) if i<r else 0; while i+z_i<n and x_{z_i}=x_{i+z_i}, increment z_i; if i+z_i>r set l=i,r=i+z_i. Return z.
variables: x finite indexed sequence; n length; z_i longest prefix matching the suffix starting at i for i>0; z_0=0 by convention; [l,r) rightmost established matching interval, possibly empty
assumptions: Immutable finite sequence, consistent equality and constant-cost indexed comparisons; exact integer indices; zero-based half-open interval convention
limitations: O(n) time and O(n) returned array storage; z_0=0 is a convention rather than a full self-match length. No approximate matching or wildcard semantics
failure_conditions: Reject inconsistent equality and unsafe index arithmetic
Do not mix inclusive and exclusive right boundaries
computation: Scan indices left to right, initialize from the known interval when inside it, extend with bounded comparisons and update the frontier. For pattern matching on a combined sequence, use a separator guaranteed unequal to all symbols and a nonempty pattern.

source.citation: Gusfield (1997), Algorithms on Strings, Trees, and Sequences, Cambridge University Press, sections 1.3–1.5, especially p. 9, Algorithm Z; adapted from one-based inclusive intervals to zero-based half-open intervals. https://dmice.ohsu.edu/bedricks/courses/cs655/pdf/readings/gusfield_chap_1_2.pdf

application: General sequence algorithm; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Finite indexed sequence with declared symbol equality.
incompatible_methods: Using an ambiguous separator for combined pattern and text
Interpreting the z array as the KMP prefix-function array without conversion
mechanism_note: Inside the established prefix-copy interval, the earlier z value certifies the minimum of that value and the remaining interval length. If strictly smaller, the mismatch lies inside the known interval; otherwise successful comparisons extend the frontier. Outside the interval successes also advance the frontier; at most one failed comparison per index. Unlike the KMP recurrence, this measures prefix matches starting at each position rather than borders ending there. Conservatively grouped as a prefix-matching variant rather than counting closely related preprocessing separately.

name: Aho–Corasick multi-pattern failure automaton
definition: Build a trie of distinct nonempty patterns. Let δ(root,a)=child(root,a) if present else root; f(root)=root and f(v)=root for root children. In breadth-first depth order, for each other edge u→v labeled a set f(v)=δ(f(u),a); for any nonroot state w set δ(w,a)=child(w,a) if present else δ(f(w),a). Set o(root)=null and o(v)=f(v) if f(v) is terminal else o(f(v)) for v≠root. Starting q=root, for each text symbol x_i set q←δ(q,x_i); report q if terminal and every terminal along the o-chain from q with ending index i.
variables: Trie states, f longest proper suffix link, δ completed transition, o nearest terminal proper suffix link, q current state; S sum of pattern lengths, K fixed alphabet size, m text length, z number of reported occurrences
assumptions: Finite fixed alphabet with constant-cost symbol indexing, finite static set of distinct nonempty patterns, exact equality, breadth-first processing and constant-cost terminal identifier emission
limitations: Dense transition table uses O((S+1)K) space and construction time; search O(m+z) with output links and constant-cost transitions. Large alphabets can make dense tables impractical; output volume can dominate. Walking all failure ancestors does not justify the same output-sensitive bound. Empty pattern set gives no matches; empty patterns excluded
failure_conditions: Reject empty patterns or symbols outside the declared alphabet
Do not follow the root failure link indefinitely
Do not omit suffix matches or overlaps
computation: Insert patterns, complete root transitions and initialize depth-one failures. Process nodes breadth-first, using already processed shallower states for failure and terminal-output links. Complete each transition row; scan text once, emitting (pattern identifier, end index) for each terminal on the output chain including the current state if terminal.

source.citation: Aho and Corasick (1975), Efficient string matching: an aid to bibliographic search, Communications of the ACM 18(6), 333–340, DOI 10.1145/360825.360855 (metadata and abstract verified; original PDF retrieval failed). Stanford CS166, Tries and String Matching, sections Suffix Links, Constructing Output Links and The Complete Construction; dense transition bound independently derived. https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs166/cs166.1146/lectures/09/Small09.pdf

application: General sequence algorithm; no empirical benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Finite sequence and finite set of nonempty patterns with declared symbol equality.
incompatible_methods: Reporting only the current state's terminal pattern
Claiming output-sensitive complexity while scanning arbitrary nonterminal failure chains
mechanism_note: The current state represents the longest suffix of processed text that is a prefix of some pattern. Failure moves to shorter represented suffixes. All matching patterns are terminal suffixes of that state, enumerated by terminal-only output links. Dense construction processes K transitions per state; output traversal visits exactly one terminal per report. A single-pattern trie specializes to the KMP failure mechanism; branching states and multiple terminal suffixes give the general automaton a distinct capability.
